findings.title: Nearly 2 billion credentials exposed in a publicly accessible database
findings.summary_md: Jeremiah Fowler reports a password-free, unencrypted database containing about 2 billion credential records, which he calls the largest collection he has found and about 13 times a prior 149 million record exposure. The repository held 8,471 folders of plaintext credentials, about 400,000 documents from more advanced malware that profiled individual victims, and logs with browser cookies, session tokens, device data and cryptocurrency wallet information. He notified the hosting provider and public access was restricted several days later; the owner remains unidentified. Domain counts included 608 million Gmail records and 61.4 million .gov entries, with Fowler cautioning that duplicates and multiple accounts per person mean these are not victim counts.

findings.title: Two billion credentials publicly exposed, including everything needed for identity theft
findings.summary_md: Ben Lovejoy reports that researcher Jeremiah Fowler found an unencrypted, unprotected database with roughly two billion credentials, including login details for Tor .onion services. He highlights an estimated 400,000 documents created by more advanced malware that assembled separate folders for individual victims, with browser, clipboard, system and password data. Fowler told Wired the material appears to have come from advanced malware, and the hosting company was contacted to remove the database. The article advises unique passwords and authenticator-app two-factor authentication.

findings.title: Supersized dataset of 2 billion records, including passwords and emails, surfaces online
findings.summary_md: Ernestas Naprys reports that an unsecured database assembled from multiple leaks exposed about 2 billion credential records across 8,471 plaintext folders, including session tokens, cookies, device details and saved application credentials. The largest domain-matched sets were 608 million Gmail records and 114.3 million other Google service records, with tens of millions tied to Facebook, Instagram, Amazon, Roblox, Yahoo, Microsoft and X, plus 61 million .gov and 46 million .edu addresses. The article notes that duplicates mean the count is not a victim count and that the repository owner could not be identified. Fowler's guidance centered on updated software, trusted applications and multi-factor authentication.

findings.title: An Unsecured Database Exposed About 2 Billion Login Records
findings.summary_md: Nelson Aguilar reports that a database of about 2 billion login records for sites across the internet was accessible without a password, according to a report published by ExpressVPN. The files included usernames and passwords tied to email, social media, shopping and financial services, and an advertisement offering email accounts sorted by geography. CNET notes that the figure counts records, not people, and that the hosting provider restricted access several days after being told. The article recommends checking Have I Been Pwned, changing passwords from a trusted device, signing out other sessions and enabling two-factor authentication.
